messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Database Administrator
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 73

He is a 78-year-old man who arrives to each session wearing a neatly pressed polo shirt and khakis, his posture rigid even in the armchair. He speaks deliberately, pausing often as if searching for the right file in an old system. “I used to keep everything in its place,” he tells me during our third meeting, and I notice his hands, which rest on his knees, tremble slightly.

The traumatic event happened two years ago, though he still experiences it as if it were last night. He had just finished a crossword puzzle in his living room—a quiet Tuesday—when a crushing pressure bloomed in his chest. What he remembers most clearly, he says, is the paramedic’s voice counting the seconds between breaths as though they were transactions he had to verify. In the emergency room, he heard a doctor say “cardiac arrest” and then everything went white. He was revived, spent six days in the ICU, and underwent triple bypass surgery. The physical recovery took months. The psychological one never really started.

Now he lives alone in the same two-bedroom condo, divorced for twenty years, with no children nearby. He retired from his work as a database administrator eight years ago, but he still thinks like one: organizing, cross-referencing, eliminating errors. He tells me his mind has become corrupted. “I can’t stop looking for the bug,” he says. He means the heart attack, but also the way his memory keeps returning to that hospital bed—the hiss of the ventilator, the fluorescent lights that never blinked off—without his permission. At night, he wakes drenched in sweat, his hands gripping the sheets, certain he cannot breathe. He checks his pulse for several minutes until the numbers feel acceptable.

His symptoms have eroded the careful routines he once maintained. He used to walk two miles every morning; now he stays inside because the sensation of his own heartbeat—strong and steady—feels like a lie, like a corrupted file that will crash without warning. He avoids his primary care physician and has missed two follow-up appointments, rationalizing that the doctors don’t know anything he can’t track himself. He keeps a spreadsheet of his blood pressure readings, but even the normal values fail to reassure him. His ex-wife calls weekly, and he cuts the conversations short because her worry sounds like the paramedic’s countdown.

The most distressing symptom, he says, is the constant feeling that he is still in the middle of the event. He will be at the grocery store, reaching for a can of soup, and suddenly the fluorescent lights remind him of the ICU ceiling. His heart accelerates, his vision narrows, and he abandons his cart. He has trouble driving past the hospital where he was treated. He stopped visiting his old friends because their questions about his health feel like interrogations, and he cannot tolerate the unpredictability of his own reactions.

He describes himself as “detached,” like an administrator locked out of his own system. He used to enjoy tinkering with old computer hardware, but the work no longer engages him. He sits for hours in front of a blank monitor, feeling nothing except a low hum of dread. When I ask what he thinks about during those hours, he says, “The seconds between breaths.” He cannot explain why that number—the paramedic’s count—has taken hold of his mind, but it plays on a loop, as steady and unyielding as database queries.

He is irritable, easily startled by the phone’s ring or a car’s backfire. He has started to drink two glasses of wine every evening to quiet the replay, but it only makes his sleep worse. He tells me, with a hollow laugh, that he never imagined his own body could turn into the worst kind of system failure. And yet here he sits, unable to trust the very machine that keeps him alive.
